Círculos y rectángulos tienen una distan: Circles and rectangles have an immediate distance; letters and icons do not. This topic closes that gap with the [[ge-vectores|projection]] of one vector onto another for segments, two rounds of interpolation for Bézier curves, and smoothstep's polynomial seen now as movement rather than as an edge.
Hasta ahora el shader sabía dibujar lo q: Up to now the shader could draw whatever has an easy distance: circles, rectangles, rings. But almost everything you see on a screen —letters, icons, strokes— is made of curves. This topic adds three pieces: the distance to a segment, the Bézier curves with which every typeface is designed, and the easing functions that make an animation look natural instead of mechanical.
Las tres son matemáticas de Bachillerato: All three are sixth-form mathematics in disguise: a [[ge-vectores|projection of one vector onto another]], a repeated interpolation and a third-degree polynomial with zero [[fn-derivadas|derivative]] at the extremes.
Para saber a qué distancia está un punto: To know how far a point $\vec p$ is from the segment running from $\vec a$ to $\vec b$, you look for the nearest point of the segment. You project $\vec p - \vec a$ onto the segment's direction, $\vec b - \vec a$, and measure what fraction $h$ of the segment has been travelled. If $h$ leaves the interval $[0, 1]$, the nearest point is an endpoint, so it is clamped. The distance is the one up to that point.
h = \\operatorname{clamp}\\left(\\frac{(: h = \operatorname{clamp}\left(\frac{(\vec p - \vec a)\cdot(\vec b - \vec a)}{(\vec b - \vec a)\cdot(\vec b - \vec a)},\ 0,\ 1\right), \qquad d = |\vec p - \vec a - h\,(\vec b - \vec a)|
distancia de un punto a un segmento: distance from a point to a segment
El cociente es el coeficiente de la proy:
The quotient is the projection's coefficient: what fraction of the segment the shadow of $\vec p - \vec a$ takes up.

$\operatorname{clamp}(x, 0, 1)$ leaves $x$ as it is if it lies between 0 and 1, and otherwise clamps it to the nearest extreme.

In GLSL it is three lines: vec2 pa = p - a, ba = b - a; float h = clamp(dot(pa, ba) / dot(ba, ba), 0.0, 1.0); return length(pa - ba * h);

Con la distancia a un segmento se dibuja: With the distance to a segment you draw any figure made of straight strokes: it is enough to keep the min of the distances to all its sides. And since it is a true distance, it serves for everything you already know how to do with distances: thickness, soft edges and haloes.

Una curva de Bézier se define con unos p: A Bézier curve is defined by a few control points. The curve starts at the first and ends at the last, but it does not pass through the middle ones: these only pull at it, like magnets. And the way to compute it is the simplest imaginable: interpolate, and interpolate again.
curvas de Bézier cuadrática y cúbica, co: quadratic and cubic Bézier curves, with t from 0 to 1
Los coeficientes de la cuadrática son lo:
The quadratic's coefficients are the terms of $\bigl((1 - t) + t\bigr)^2$, the [[al-identidades|square of a binomial]], and the cubic's, those of its cube: 1, 3, 3, 1. Since $(1 - t) + t = 1$, they always add up to 1: the point on the curve is a weighted average of the control points, and that is why the curve stays inside the polygon they form.

In GLSL, the quadratic is mix(mix(P0, P1, t), mix(P1, P2, t), t): two rounds of interpolation.

Las curvas de Bézier llevan el nombre de: Bézier curves are named after Pierre Bézier, a Renault engineer who used and popularised them in the 1960s to design car bodies with the first computers. But Paul de Casteljau, a Citroën mathematician, had reached the same thing in 1959, with the interpolate-and-interpolate-again algorithm that bears his name. Citroën kept it an industrial secret for years, and that is why the fame went to the man from the competition.
Todas las letras que estás leyendo son c: Every letter you are reading is Bézier curves: TrueType typefaces use quadratics and OpenType ones with PostScript outlines, cubics. The paths of illustration programs, the paths of an SVG file and the cubic-bezier function with which a web page's animations are defined are the same formula.
Una animación en la que algo se mueve a: An animation in which something moves at constant speed and stops abruptly looks robotic. Real objects start little by little and brake little by little. To imitate that, instead of moving something in proportion to the time $x$, you move it according to a function $f(x)$ that goes from 0 to 1 with another shape. The most used is smoothstep, and it is not magic: it is a polynomial.
Vale 0 en $x = 0$ y 1 en $x = 1$, igual:
It is 0 at $x = 0$ and 1 at $x = 1$, just like the line $f(x) = x$. The difference is in the [[fn-derivadas|derivative]]: $f'(0) = f'(1) = 0$. The speed is zero on leaving and on arriving, and maximum in the middle, where $f'(\frac{1}{2}) = \frac{3}{2}$.

With other edges, $x$ is first taken to the interval $[0, 1]$: smoothstep(e0, e1, x) uses $t = \operatorname{clamp}\left(\frac{x - e_0}{e_1 - e_0}, 0, 1\right)$ and returns $3t^2 - 2t^3$.
velocidad constante, arranque y frenazo: constant speed, abrupt start and stop
arranca deprisa y frena al llegar: starts fast and brakes on arrival
Las cuatro bolas hacen el mismo recorrid: The four balls make the same journey in the same time, there and back. From top to bottom: linear, ease in, ease out and smoothstep. Notice how the sense of weight changes even though all of them take the same time.
